summary:
Same-sex conduct between adults is legal in Madagascar, but only from age 21. Penal Code Article 331 treats same-sex acts involving a person under 21 as indecent assault, with a reported penalty band of five to ten years' imprisonment. The age of consent is therefore unequal: a visitor whose partner or counterparty is under 21 faces a serious criminal exposure that a heterosexual visitor does not, and a 2020 case shows the provision reaching a consensual same-sex relationship between a 33-year-old and a 19-year-old woman after a complaint by the younger woman's mother.

Marriage is closed to same-sex couples. Article 2 of Law No. 2007-022 on Marriage and Matrimonial Regimes prohibits marriage between two persons of the same sex, whether before the Civil Registrar or under traditional ceremonies. Article 39 of the same law names gender identity as a cause for absolute nullity of marriage, which is a direct legal exposure for a trans visitor whose relationship status is examined locally.

Adoption is closed on the same basis. Article 33 of Law No. 2005-014 on Adoption states that full adoption is permitted only to heterosexual spouses.

Public expression of LGBT identity is constrained by authorities rather than by a general ban. In early July 2021 the Malagasy government cancelled an LGBTQ party held at a bar in Antananarivo on the grounds of incitement to debauchery, so a visitor attending or organising an identifiable LGBT event can expect the event to be shut down and participants recorded.

Violence against LGBT people, and against transgender people in particular, is documented. The 2011 U.S. State Department Human Rights Report recorded societal discrimination with public attitudes ranging from tacit acceptance to violent rejection, singling out transgender sex workers as frequent targets of verbal abuse, stone throwing and even murder. Supporters of a same-sex couple received insults and death threats on social media, and religious leaders publicly accused them of promoting homosexuality.

The government's official posture at the United Nations is one of refusal. In Madagascar's fourth Universal Periodic Review in January 2025, covering 235 recommendations, the government rejected UN recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent.

Concealment is the ordinary practice. A France 24 report from 2024 found that although homosexuality is not illegal, it is widely considered socially unacceptable, and many LGBT people hide their sexuality to keep their jobs and live in peace, relying on their own networks and coded language.
tangentialFactors:
Madagascar is one of a substantial group of African states that has decriminalised same-sex conduct: as of July 2020, about 22 of 53 states on the continent had moved to decriminalise, with Madagascar's contribution limited to the over-21 position of its Penal Code rather than a full equalisation.

Two statutes treat sexual life and sexual orientation as protected personal data. Article 18 of Law No. 2014-038 on the Protection of Personal Data bars processing of sensitive data including data on health or sexual life, and Article 2 of Law No. 2017-045 on Credit Information Bureaus likewise protects sexual orientation as sensitive data. Neither provision creates a right of recognition or disclosure, but both constrain how far private-sector and administrative handlers may record a visitor's orientation.

The 2011 human rights reporting period fell under the post-coup regime, which was characterised by unlawful killings; that context shaped the state's documented capacity to investigate and punish violence against LGBT people. Comparative guides rate the legal framework as limited in progress against neighbouring countries, with civic rights such as marriage and adoption absent rather than contested.

Social attitudes vary sharply by setting. The same reporting places public opinion across a band running from tacit acceptance to violent rejection, so the practical risk to a visitor depends heavily on visibility, locality and the presence of religious or community figures willing to publicise a relationship.
localsOnly:
Law No. 2005-014 on Adoption restricts full adoption to heterosexual spouses, and Law No. 2007-022 closes marriage to same-sex couples before the Civil Registrar and under traditional ceremonies, leaving Malagasy same-sex couples with no route to either status.

Act No. 2005-040 on the Fight against HIV/AIDS requires information, education and communication programmes adapted to the sexual orientation of the target groups, and Article 26 mandates special provisions to protect vulnerable groups, expressly including young people, sex workers, men who have sex with men and mobile populations, against HIV transmission.

The 2020 statutory-rape case illustrates how the Penal Code's indecent-assault provisions are used domestically: a 33-year-old woman was arrested over her relationship with a 19-year-old woman after the younger woman's mother filed a complaint, in circumstances where the mother was alleged to be covering up an incest and rape accusation against the father. Religious leaders subsequently offered the young woman conversion therapy.

Six Malagasy organisations — Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers' Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage and Madagascar LGBT+ — publicly protested the January 2025 UPR outcome, stating that refusing to act is to endorse impunity and condone violence.

Domestic employment and social standing depend on concealment: LGBT Malagasy described hiding their sexuality to keep jobs and sustain ordinary community life, working through private networks and coded language.
outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty band attached to Penal Code Article 331 is reported inconsistently across the sources in the inventory, with one giving five to ten years' imprisonment for indecent assault involving a person under 21 and another indicating a two-to-five-year band for indecent or against-nature acts. The discrepancy is unresolved here; a visitor relying on the exact sentence should check the current consolidated text of the Penal Code.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa rules, airport or border screening, gender markers on passports or other travel documents, or the placement of trans detainees, so no finding is recorded on those points.

Whether Madagascar has a hate-crime statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity is not sourced. The inventory documents social media death threats and violence but no prosecution or acquittal under a specific aggravated-offence provision.

Recognition of foreign same-sex marriages, foreign partner visas and inheritance or hospital-visitation rights for foreign same-sex partners are not covered by any source here and remain unresolved.

No source addresses facilities access, healthcare refusal on gender-identity grounds beyond the HIV framework, or the practical availability of trans-competent medical care.
